cards.explanation: The answer is foes, friends. David opens with, "O LORD, how my foes have increased!" (Psalm 3:1). He doesn't dress it up or pretend things are fine. He just tells the LORD how things really are, and I think that's a good way to start a prayer.

The answer is that they say, “God will not deliver him.” That's what many are saying about David (Psalm 3:2). It's a heavy thing to hear about yourself. Notice that David tells it to God and doesn't keep it to himself, friends.

The answer is a shield, friends. David says, "But You, O LORD, are a shield around me…" (Psalm 3:3). Look at that word "around." I think a shield you can hold in front of you is good, but one all the way around is even better.

The answer is True, friends. David says the LORD is “…my glory, and the One who lifts my head.” (Psalm 3:3). Just before that, the psalm reports what many say about him. I think a lifted head is a mighty fine thing to have in a rough week.
The answer is False, friends. David says, "To the LORD I cry aloud, and He answers me from His holy mountain." (Psalm 3:4). He cries out, and the LORD answers. I love that David didn't mumble it.

The reason David gives is that the LORD sustains him. He says, "I lie down and sleep; I wake again, for the LORD sustains me." (Psalm 3:5). Lie down, sleep, wake up, and the reason is the LORD. I'd sleep better with that reason, honestly, friends.
The word is fear, friends. David says, "I will not fear the myriads set against me on every side." (Psalm 3:6). Myriads means a huge number, and he still says it. That's some steady courage.
David asks God to save him, friends. He prays, "Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God!" (Psalm 3:7). It's short and it's direct. I like a prayer that gets right to it.

The answer is True, and it's right there in the text, friends. David prays, "Strike all my enemies on the jaw…" (Psalm 3:7). It's blunt, and he says it to the LORD. I think that's honest praying, with nothing held back.

The answer is the LORD, friends. David says, “Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people.” (Psalm 3:8). After all that talk of enemies, he lands on who saves, and then he prays for God's people. It's a great last line.

The answer is False, friends. David closes with, "Salvation belongs to the LORD; may Your blessing be on Your people." (Psalm 3:8). He asks for blessing on God's people, not just on himself. A prayer that began with his foes ends with the whole people of God.
